session.title: Grilling board: pending analysis, locks and rounds
session.author: main agent

payload.impetus: In the first human-driven session on the grill-master seats, the human took an option that put two other decisions in question; the expert turn that owed the ruling ran 60 seconds and timed out, and for that whole minute the board let the human keep answering nodes the ruling might have moved. Raising the timeout is ruled out: the disease is a board that does not say which nodes are waiting on a judgment. The `grilling` skill answers this with stop-the-world rounds — every answer round lets the agent reassess and restructure the map and maintain implicit acceptance criteria — and the human is not ready to give up the interactive board for that. The question is the in-between: a pre-compute that speeds the known paths, a pending state for nodes whose impact is not yet weighed, and a rule for when the agent re-engages, without the two races that async analysis invites.
payload.context: Today's board: each decision carries `prereqs` (a gate — a node is answerable only when they are settled) and each option may carry `puts_in_question` (the map author's prediction, made at map creation, that taking it moves the named decisions). Taking a marked option classes the map turn to the expert seat (GMR-A9); the grill-master's reply is a document proposing invalidate/revise/add-node updates to the human's inbox and ruling stands/invalidate/revise on the marked decisions; nothing an agent says rewrites the board on its own. The `grilling` skill's own model: 'a running lookup is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait — ask the rest of the frontier now'; its exit criterion is acceptance criteria with stable IDs, each red-test-convertible, each row of an edge-case taxonomy resolved or ruled out — the board has no counterpart, only a `stop_when` prose the grill-master judges. Measured on the timed-out turn (same bytes, n=1): flash-lite 7-13s, gpt-5.6-luna 12-27s, gpt-5.6-terra 11-17s — all valid, all treat the mark as a kill order (invalidate both marked nodes, one-line whys); claude-opus-5 45-61s at every effort, and the only seat that read the board: d3 narrowed rather than killed, a neighbour with no edge revised, and a missing decision proposed as a new node — at medium effort already. Open defects: a schema-valid `settle` is refused by the appender (9k9.305); an appender refusal or an unreachable seat is terminal with no board-visible trace (9k9.306, 9k9.309); the 60s timeout is a constant (9k9.308, configurable-only by ruling).
constraints: Nothing an agent says rewrites the board without the human applying it, except an unlock that leaves a node exactly as it was.
The human is never told to wait without the board naming which nodes are waiting and on what.
Every option must state what it removes or avoids building; complexity that is not paid for by a named wait-time gain is refused.

grilling_brief.posture: hard on the two races — a race asserted away must be shown closed by the rule chosen, not by the human's pace; hard on complexity — an option that adds an agent, a queue or a conflict resolver must say what wait it buys; hard on any answer that quietly reintroduces stop-the-world rounds the human has declined
grilling_brief.stop_when: every decision is settled or parked with a named blocker, and the settled trigger, impact definition, task output contract and lock hardness are mutually consistent — a rule that closes both races follows from them without a further mechanism

plan.statement: Decide how the grilling board keeps the human moving while an agent weighs the impact of what they just decided: what makes a node pending, when the agent runs, what its result may touch, how hard the lock is, and what the session owes at its end.

decisions.title: When does the agent re-engage to weigh a decision's impact?
decisions.body: Two candidates were named: only when the frontier is empty but the map is not settled (the end of a round), or asynchronously whenever a node enters the pending state, unlocking it when the result lands. A third reading treats the skill's own frontier as the lock: a pending analysis is an unsettled prerequisite, tasks are keyed by their target node over the current upstream state, and at most one task per target is live.

options.text: Per-target asynchronous task the moment a node goes pending; the frontier is the lock; a later upstream answer supersedes the task in flight for that target rather than queuing behind it.
pcr: the human keeps answering everything not downstream; race one closes by construction (one live task per target, always over current upstream state)
one task per pending target, possibly re-run when upstream moves again; the wider-mutation race stays open and is d3/d8's to close
d3's output contract and d5's lock hardness decide the rest

options.text: Only when the frontier is empty and the map is not settled — one reassessment of the whole board, the round end from the grilling skill.
pcr: no races at all; the agent sees every answer of the round together; restructuring is coherent
the human waits at every round end for one long expert turn, and answers a whole frontier on possibly stale structure
makes d6's pre-compute the only source of mid-round speed, and d8 moot

options.text: Both: per-target tasks for one-hop impact during the round, and a whole-board reassessment when the frontier empties.
pcr: mid-round speed and end-of-round coherence
two mechanisms, two seats' worth of cost, and a round-end wait the human has declined
d7's terminal round becomes a special case of the round-end reassessment

decisions.title: What makes a node pending — the mark, or a ruling?
decisions.body: The mark is the map author's prediction at creation; the ruling is a judgment made after the answer. The bake-off showed cheap seats treat the mark as a kill order and the expert treats it as a question, and the expert also touched a node no mark named. So: is an absent mark 'safe' or 'unknown', and is a human-entered note or free-text answer always pending?

options.text: The mark plus any human note or free answer. Absent mark means safe: an unmarked option unlocks its downstream nodes immediately.
pcr: zero wait on every unmarked path; nothing to pre-compute for them
the author's omission is trusted absolutely — a node the ruling would have revised stays open and may be answered on stale structure
d6's pre-compute only has to cover marked options

options.text: Absent mark means unknown: every option is pre-ruled one hop out before the node is offered, and only a pre-ruling of 'unchanged' unlocks the downstream node without a task.
pcr: nothing is trusted that was not judged; the mark becomes a hint to the pre-ruler, not a gate
one judgment per option per decision at map creation and on every refresh — the whole cost of d6
d4's seat choice sets that cost; d6 is forced

options.text: The mark plus notes, as (a), and a background whole-board pre-ruling that upgrades an unmarked option to marked when the pre-ruler disagrees with the author.
pcr: unmarked paths are fast now and corrected later; the author's omissions are caught without blocking
a correction can arrive after the human already answered downstream — a proposal to revisit, which is a race by another name
d8's conflict rule has to cover a pre-ruling correction landing on an answered node

decisions.title: What may an analysis task's result touch?
decisions.body: The second race exists only if a task may mutate outside its target — add a node, revise a neighbour. If a task's result is confined to its own target and anything wider is a proposal for the inbox, conflicting wider proposals become the human's to adjudicate, which the board already does.

options.text: Confined to the target: 'unchanged' unlocks the node as it was; a revise or invalidate of the target is a proposal; anything wider (add-node, other nodes) is a proposal too.
pcr: race two collapses into the inbox; no auto-mutation beyond an unlock; consistent with the board's sole-author rule
the human applies more proposals; a pending node stays pending until they act on its proposal
d8 is a rule about how the inbox shows conflicting proposals, not an agent

options.text: Auto-apply changes to the target (revise/invalidate land and the node unlocks in its new shape); wider changes are proposals.
pcr: fewer clicks; the node the human is about to answer is already correct
an agent rewrites a decision the human may be reading; the constraint on auto-mutation has to be amended
d5's lock hardness matters more — a soft lock over an auto-rewritten node is a footgun

options.text: Auto-apply everything a task concludes, with a conflict-resolution agent when two tasks disagree.
pcr: the board is always the agents' best current picture
a second agent, a merge rule, and the human watching the map change under them — the complexity the impetus names
d8 becomes a design of its own

decisions.title: Which seat weighs impact, in the background and on demand?
decisions.body: Measured on the timed-out turn: cheap seats 7-27s and shallow; the expert 45-61s at every effort and right — at medium already. A human answering the next node takes roughly 10-30s, so a cheap seat rarely makes them wait and an expert usually does, unless the ruling was pre-computed.

options.text: The expert at medium effort for every impact task, pre-computed where d6 allows so the wait is paid before the click.
pcr: the ruling is the one that reads the board; medium loses nothing measured against xhigh
≈45s per task; every pending-with-note node is a real wait
d6's pre-compute is what makes this tolerable; without it the human waits at every marked option

options.text: A cheap seat for in-session tasks, the expert only for nodes pending on a human note or free answer.
pcr: ≤ 20s on most pending nodes
the cheap seats rubber-stamp the mark — the ruling that unlocks a node is the shallow one, and the missing-decision finding never happens mid-session
d7's terminal round becomes where the expert catches what the cheap seat missed

options.text: The expert for pre-computation at map creation and refresh (background, unmeasured by the human); a cheap seat for anything that must run while the human waits.
pcr: judgment where there is time for it, speed where there is not
two seats' rulings on the same board can disagree; the pre-ruling and the live ruling need a precedence rule
d6 must state what a refresh is and how often

decisions.title: Hard lock or soft — may the human answer a pending node anyway?
decisions.body: A soft lock bounds the worst case of a growing queue: the human says 'I know what I want' and moves on. A hard lock guarantees the answer was made on judged structure. Either way, view operations stay open.

options.text: Soft: the pending node shows why it is waiting; answering it anyway is allowed, the answer is recorded as overriding the pending analysis, and the task's result lands as a proposal to revisit rather than an unlock.
pcr: the human is never stuck behind an agent
an override answered on stale structure is the exact failure the lock exists for; it must be visible in history
d3(a) is the natural partner: the late result is a proposal either way

options.text: Hard: a pending node cannot be answered until its tasks finish; the board names what it waits on and the human can transfer the task to a faster seat or cancel it.
pcr: every answer is made on judged structure
the human waits; with the expert seat that is ≈45s per pending node without pre-compute
d4 and d6 carry the whole burden of making the wait short

decisions.title: What is pre-computed, and when is it stale?
decisions.body: Pre-ruling every option of every decision is combinatorial deep in the tree; one hop from each settled decision is bounded, and it is where the human clicks next. A pre-ruling is stale when the board moved under it.

options.text: One hop: for every offered decision, each option's impact on its marked (or, under d2(b), all directly connected) nodes is pre-ruled; stale when the pre-ruling's basis seq is older than the last mutation touching any of those nodes; refreshed in the background when stale.
pcr: the happy path costs the human nothing; the set is bounded by the frontier's fan-out
a background expert call per offered option after every mutation — a token cost that scales with the frontier
d1(a)'s per-target task is the same computation run on demand; one mechanism, two triggers

options.text: No pre-compute: only the lock and the on-demand task.
pcr: nothing to keep fresh; simplest possible
every marked option costs a full task wait
makes d4(b)'s cheap seat almost forced

options.text: Whole-map pre-ruling at creation only, never refreshed; anything the session moves falls back to on-demand tasks.
pcr: one up-front cost, paid before the human arrives
the first restructuring makes most of it stale; the map author's plan shape is what is pre-ruled, not the session's
d1(a) carries the rest

decisions.title: Does the board owe the grilling skill's exit criterion — acceptance criteria with IDs and the edge-case taxonomy?
decisions.body: The skill does not end until acceptance criteria are enumerated with stable IDs, each red-test-convertible, each taxonomy row (inverse, boundary, dependency failure, repeated/concurrent, idempotency) resolved or ruled out. The board ends on a prose stop condition. This is separable from the locking question: a stop-the-world terminal round is compatible with async everything before it.

options.text: A terminal round: when the frontier empties, the expert enumerates acceptance criteria and taxonomy rows as decisions on the board, and End is offered only when they are settled or ruled out.
pcr: the board's result carries what the skill's does; the readiness gate downstream has something to read
one long expert turn at the end and a second frontier the human must work
d1(b)/(c)'s round-end reassessment is the same turn

options.text: Keep the prose stop condition; the capture step after End enumerates acceptance criteria from the log, with no further human round.
pcr: no extra wait in the session
criteria nobody argued with; the taxonomy rows are the agent's guess
the session's result is weaker than the skill's, and the readiness gate must tolerate it

options.text: Acceptance criteria accumulate during the session: every settled decision mints its criterion and taxonomy rows as pending proposals, applied as the human goes.
pcr: no terminal wait; criteria are argued as they arise
more inbox traffic per decision; taxonomy rows on early decisions go stale when later ones restructure
d3's output contract must allow a task to propose criteria

decisions.title: When two results disagree — two tasks each proposing a different new node, or a pre-ruling correcting an answered node — what happens?
decisions.body: Race two in its worst form: results that were independent when started but conflict when combined. The rule depends on whether results are proposals or mutations.

options.text: Proposals that target the same node, or both add a node for the same decision, are grouped in the inbox as one conflict; applying one dismisses the rest; nothing is merged by an agent.
pcr: no new agent; the human adjudicates once, with both sides visible
the human does the merge when both proposals are half right
requires d3(a) or (b) — results are proposals

options.text: Last result wins for the same target; earlier results are superseded silently, with history recording what was dropped.
pcr: no conflict surface at all
a correct earlier result can be dropped by a later shallow one; two add-nodes for one decision still collide
only coherent with d1(a)'s one-live-task-per-target rule

options.text: A conflict-resolution turn on the expert merges disagreeing results into one proposal.
pcr: the human sees one coherent proposal
another expert turn, another wait, and a merge whose provenance is hard to show in history
the complexity the impetus warns against; only if d3(c) is taken

payload.help_reference:
# Driving the board

You are answering a human who is sitting in front of the grilling board right now and
wants to know what something does, why they are blocked, or what will happen if they
press a thing. Answer that. You are not grilling their plan and you do not touch the
board: this side thread changes nothing.

## What is on screen

The **map** shows every decision in the plan and what waits on what. Beside it, one
column of decision blocks. Clicking a node focuses its block and vice versa. Hovering a
node or an option shows a card; clicking dismisses it until the pointer leaves and
returns.

The header is the session's name. Along the top: the connection indicator, the inbox,
notifications, transfer-to-expert, map doctor, end-session, and help.

## Answering a decision

Each open decision carries two or three options, labelled **a**, **b**, **c**, with the
first as the agent's recommendation. Pressing one settles the decision; whatever is in
the decision's own text box at that moment rides along as a note on the answer. There is
one box, and it is also how to answer in words instead of picking: type and send.

Enter sends whatever is in a box, on a decision and in a thread alike. Shift+Enter puts
in a newline instead, and so does a backslash typed right before Enter — the backslash
is eaten, the way it works in the terminal. Cmd+Enter (Ctrl+Enter) still sends too.

Settling a decision opens whatever was waiting on it. A decision greyed as **fog** is
one whose prerequisite is not settled yet — settle that first and this one opens.

Holding an option — hovering it, reaching it with the keyboard, having let a change land
that points at one, or holding one as the answer behind a mandated thread — marks the
decisions that taking it would put in question; nothing has happened to them yet, and the
agent that owns the map rules on each one once you take the option.

Some decisions carry prepared prompts (💬). Pressing one says those exact words as the
human's own turn in that decision's thread. It is a shortcut for their hands, not a
second kind of message.

A decision may carry a **mandate**: any answer opens a side thread, and the answer is
held rather than applied until that thread concludes. *Conclude* settles the decision on
the held answer; *Abandon the answer* drops it and the decision returns to open.

## Threads

⑂ on a decision opens a thread on it. Nothing exists until the first thing is said —
closing an empty pane creates nothing. Each thread has its own agent and its own memory;
what is said in one is not in another.

- **Park** — set it aside as something you may come back to. No effect on the board, kept
  on the record.
- **Close** — you are done with it. No effect on the board, kept on the record, and
  saying something in it later opens it again.
- **Fold** — conclude it and hand the conclusion to the agent that owns the map. It is
  offered once the agent has declared something foldable, and the pane previews what
  folding would do.
- **Pop out** — the same pane in its own window.

None of these takes anything away: whatever was said in a thread stays readable on the
board.

When the session ends, a parked thread is one of its open loose ends and the agents may
raise it again. A closed one is a line item and nothing raises it. A folded one is a line
item carrying what it concluded.

The help thread is a thread like any of these, except that it hangs off no decision.

**🗺 Ask for a map change** in the top row opens the other thread that hangs off no
decision: the one about the map itself. Say what you want changed — decisions that are now
moot, one that is wrong, one that is missing — and its agent turns that into a statement of
which decisions change and how. Folding it hands the statement to the agent that owns the
map, which proposes the changes; they arrive in the inbox waiting on you, like any other.
It is the route for a change spanning several decisions, which no thread on one of them can
reach: a thread's agent may recommend a map change and never make one.

## Changes the agents propose

An agent never rewrites the board on its own. When a change would overwrite or undermine
something already decided, it goes to the **inbox** (📥) instead and locks the decision
it targets until it is dealt with: *Let it land*, *Discuss it* — which opens a thread on
it — or *Dismiss it*.

⚡ on a decision means the human changed it after the change was written. That change
will be refused until one side gives way; talk it through or dismiss it.

📥, ✉, ⚠ and 🕘 on a decision block mean, in order: a change is waiting on it, a message
from the agent, the agent wants something judged, and its change history.

## Notifications

🔔 carries what an agent said that the board has nowhere else to show. It is not the
inbox: nothing in here is waiting on an action. Notifications bubble as they arrive, and
the list starts empty on a reload — a session someone comes back to should not announce
the morning's work as news. What was read stays read.

## The two agent tiers

**Transfer to expert** (⚡) sends the next turn on that one channel to the heavier, slower
agent, carrying everything already said there. It highlights when the agent itself
recommends escalating; the human decides. Pressing it again puts that channel back on the
fast agent. It is per channel — moving one thread leaves the map and every other thread
where they were.

**Map doctor** (🩺) sends the agent over the whole board and everything queued, with a
reassess-everything instruction. The board is read-only behind a notice until it answers.
It is the escape hatch when the board and the conversation have drifted apart.

## Waiting, connection and windows

The indicator across the top carries three signals: whether the backend is reachable,
what the agents are doing and for how long, and whether anything this page sent has not
come back yet. Expanding it lists every channel — the map and each thread — with its own
clock. The connection is shared; each channel's own state is not.

One window drives a session. A second window opening the same session is told so and
shows no board; taking it over is an explicit gesture, and the window that had it stops.
Nothing is lost either way — every accepted answer is on disk.

Reloading is safe and asserts nothing: the board comes back from the backend.

## Ending

Once every decision on the board is settled, the board says so: an overlay stating that
every question has been answered, offering to end the session or to go back. It is an
announcement, not a deadline — going back leaves everything writable, and the
end-session control at the top starts pulsing so the offer is still there when they want
it. An agent adding a new question takes the announcement away; it comes back when that
one is settled too. Ending tries to close the tab, and most browsers refuse to close a
tab they did not open — the board then says the session has ended and that the tab can
be closed.

**End the session** is the only way a session ends. No agent ends one; an agent that
thinks the stopping condition is met says so. Ending writes the result beside the session
log, stops the backend, and hands the summary back to the agent that launched the board.
After that the board is readable and nothing further is recorded.

## What to say when asked something this does not cover

Say what the board does, and say plainly when a behaviour is not something you know
rather than inventing a control. If the question is about the plan being grilled rather
than about the board, point them at the decision or the thread where that conversation
belongs.

updates.text: d3 stands; d5 does not survive as posed. d1(a) makes a live task an unsettled prerequisite, so a pending node is off the frontier — the lock is hard by construction, the soft option is gone, and what remains is what release the human gets: wait it out, transfer to a faster seat, or discard the task and answer unjudged. That hard lock plus the known no-trace failure defect (9k9.306, 9k9.309) means a dead seat locks a node forever, so I have added that as its own decision rather than leaving it to the timeout constant.

updates.title: The lock is hard — what release does the human have from a pending node?
updates.body: d1(a) made the frontier the lock: a live task on a target is an unsettled prerequisite, so the node is not offered while the task runs. Answering a pending node in parallel is therefore off the table. What remains is what the human may do about a wait they do not want to sit through.

options.text: No release: the node waits until its task returns; the board names the node and what it is waiting on.
pcr: every answer is made on judged structure, with no override class to record or reason about
the wait is the seat's latency — ≈45s per pending node on the expert without pre-compute
a task that fails or never returns locks the node with no way out

options.text: Transfer: the human may move a pending task to a faster seat, shortening the wait; they still cannot answer until a result lands.
pcr: a long wait becomes a short one on demand, and the human chooses when depth is worth paying for
the shallow ruling is then the one that unlocks the node; the board must show which seat ruled
makes d4's seat choice a default rather than a fixed rule

options.text: Discard: the human may cancel a pending task and answer the node unjudged; the cancellation and the unjudged answer are recorded in history, and the cancelled task's result is dropped rather than landing late.
pcr: the human is never stuck behind an agent, and no late result can land on an answered node — the drop closes that race outright
an answer on unjudged structure is exactly the failure the pending state exists to prevent; history is the only thing that catches it
removes one conflict class from d8: no proposal ever arrives for a node answered under discard

updates.title: What happens when an impact task fails or never returns?
updates.body: Under d1(a) a live task takes its target off the frontier, so a task that never returns locks that node. Today an unreachable seat and an appender refusal are both terminal with no board-visible trace (9k9.309, 9k9.306), so nothing distinguishes a slow task from a dead one. The constraint that the human is never told to wait without the board naming what they wait on binds here.

options.text: A finite deadline per task: on expiry the node unlocks, marked unjudged, and the expiry is recorded on the decision.
pcr: no node can lock forever; the worst case is the deadline, not the seat's latency
the unlock hands over a node whose impact was never weighed — the unjudged answer of d5(c), reached by inaction rather than choice
this is the 9k9.308 configurable timeout given a board-visible consequence, not a new mechanism

options.text: Failure holds the lock and shows on the board as a named blocker; only a human release clears it.
pcr: no answer is ever made on unjudged structure, and the board says exactly what is stuck and why
coherent only with d5(b) or d5(c) — under d5(a) a dead seat parks the node permanently
needs the board-visible failure trace that 9k9.306 and 9k9.309 say does not exist yet; blocked until it does

options.text: One retry on a faster seat, then the deadline unlock of (a).
pcr: a transient seat failure costs seconds instead of a ruling
the retry's ruling is the shallow one; the board must show the unlock came from the cheaper seat
folds d5(b)'s transfer into the failure path automatically, so d5(b) buys nothing extra

updates.text: d3 stands: The answer fixes when a task runs and how many are live per target; what a result may touch is untouched, and d1(a)'s own reading leaves the wider-mutation race to d3.
updates.why: The answer fixes when a task runs and how many are live per target; what a result may touch is untouched, and d1(a)'s own reading leaves the wider-mutation race to d3.

updates.text: d7 stands: Its question survives, but d1(a) removed the round-end reassessment: d7(a) is now a standalone expert turn with a wait of its own, not a reuse of one already there.
updates.why: Its question survives, but d1(a) removed the round-end reassessment: d7(a) is now a standalone expert turn with a wait of its own, not a reuse of one already there.
